claims.text: The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy has a single-phase BCC structure.
The baseline alloy has high density.
The baseline alloy has insufficient room-temperature ductility and fails at low strain.
A minor Si addition will induce a secondary intermetallic phase in the Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy.
The Si-induced secondary phase may be a Laves phase or a silicide such as (Hf,Ti,Zr)2Si.
The secondary intermetallic precipitates will form a continuous or semi-continuous reticulated network within the BCC matrix.
The reticulated intermetallic network will act as a physical barrier to crack propagation.
The network will force cracks to deflect, branch, or arrest.
Crack deflection, branching, or arrest will increase fracture toughness and room-temperature compressive ductility.
Si retained in solid solution will contribute to yield-strength enhancement.
Si addition will produce a measurable increase in room-temperature compressive plastic strain relative to the baseline.
Si addition will increase room-temperature compressive yield strength relative to the baseline.
The Si-modified alloy will have a density increase of less than 1.5% relative to the baseline.
The predicted density change is attributed to Si having low atomic weight relative to the Hf/Zr-rich matrix.
Keeping the Si concentration below approximately 2 at.% avoids crossing a percolation threshold for catastrophic embrittlement.
The cooling rate determines whether a reticulated network forms rather than coarse, isolated intermetallic particles.
A 0.5 at.% Mn addition can serve as a non-intermetallic-forming, solid-solution-strengthening comparator.
The proposed effects are to be evaluated under room-temperature uniaxial compression.
